The present application under Section 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been filed by the State seeking leave to prefer an appeal against the judgment dated 29.01.2019 passed by learned Sessions Judge, Datia in Sessions Trial No.34/2018, whereby the respondent-accused was acquitted of the charge under Section 306 of IPC.

As per the prosecution case, the deceased, Rajni Kevat, was a widow, and the accused, Ravi Kevat,
was a widower.
They married on 31.12.2015 through a notarized contract in Jhansi Tehsil and were living together as husband and wife.
It was alleged that the accused, being addicted to alcohol, used to harass the deceased and threaten her life.

On 12.02.2017, after an altercation and verbal abuse,
the deceased allegedly committed suicide by hanging herself.
Following her death, a case was registered under Section 174 CrPC, and after investigation, a case was registered against the accused under Sections 306, 498A, and 323 IPC.
Statements were recorded, the scene NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:3724 2 MCRC-16263-2019 was surveyed, and the post-mortem was conducted before submission of the charge sheet.

Vide order dated 20.02.2018, the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Datia, after evaluating the oral and medical evidence, concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove the allegations beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the accused.
The State filed a revision before the Sessions Court, Datia, which was also dismissed vide judgment dated 29.01.2019.
Aggrieved, the State had filed the present petition seeking leave to appeal.

Learned counsel for the State has contended that the judgment of acquittal passed by the learned Trial Court is contrary to law and the evidence on record and is liable to be set aside, as the father The State Of Madhya Pradesh vs Ravi on 29 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161636603/

sentences.text: After the marriage, Ravi, who was addicted to alcohol
, regularly assaulted and harassed Rajni, threatening her life.

On 12.02.2017,
after an altercation in which Ravi verbally abused Rajni, she became distressed and subsequently committed suicide by hanging.
It is furtther submitted that the post-mortem examination conducted by Dr. Anil Jain confirmed that the cause of death was asphyxia due to ligature strangulation.
Other witnesses, including the deceased's brother-in-law, corroborated the harassment and threats made by the accused.
It is therefore prayed that leave to appeal be granted, and the accused persons be convicted and sentenced.

Having considered the submissions of learned counsel for the State and perused the entire record,
this Court finds that both the learned Judicial NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:3724 3 MCRC-16263-2019 Magistrate First Class, Bhind, as well as the learned Sessions Judge, Datia, have meticulously examined the prosecution evidence and evaluated the testimonies of the witnesses.

The record reveals that the respondent had only uttered stray and casual remarks such as "why don't you die" during a quarrel, which, by themselves, do not constitute instigation within the meaning of Section 107 of the Indian Penal Code.
Such expressions, though undesirable and insensitive, were made in the heat of the moment and lack the element of mens rea necessary to drive the deceased to commit suicide.
Instigation necessarily involves a positive act of encouragement, provocation, or intentional aid with the clear objective of compelling a person to take the extreme step.

Mere abusive language, casual remarks, or general harassment, unless shown to be of such gravity and continuity as to leave the deceased with no option except to commit suicide, cannot be construed as abetment.

In the present case, there is no material on record to demonstrate that the alleged utterances were accompanied by any deliberate or persistent conduct on the part of the respondent which could be said to have created a situation of such unbearable mental cruelty that the deceased was compelled to end her life.
The evidence also does not establish a proximate and live link between the alleged words spoken by the respondent and the act of suicide.

Therefore, in the absence of intentional instigation, active participation, or any positive act facilitating the commission of suicide, the alleged utterances attributed to the respondent fall short of the statutory requirements of abetment, and cannot sustain a conviction under Section 306 IPC.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:3724 4 MCRC-16263-2019
It is further evident from the record that the evidence presented was not wholly consistent and contained certain contradictions and omissions.

The courts below have, therefore, taken a cautious and balanced approach in assessing the reliability and credibility of the evidence, and have arrived at a conclusion that the prosecution has failed to establish the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
The view adopted by the courts below is a reasonable and plausible conclusion based on the evidence on record.

In the absence of any finding that is perverse, arbitrary, or wholly unsustainable, this Court finds no justification to interfere with the acquittal in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction under Section 378(3) of the CrPC.

The Court reiterates that an appeal against acquittal requires a strong and compelling reason to set aside the findings of fact recorded by the courts below, which is not forthcoming in the present case.
